title: Nathan Fielder Reveals Unconventional Doc Tricks in “You Can See Everything” – Hollywood Reporter Exclusive
body:
The buzz surrounding “You Can See Everything,” the documentary co‑directed by comedian‑turned‑filmmaker Nathan Fielder, reached a new pitch at the Savannah College of Art and Design (SCAD) Film Festival on Wednesday, where Fielder fielded his first live interview about the film’s unconventional storytelling methods. The documentary, which chronicles the rise and fall of Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has already broken box‑office records for a nonfiction feature, prompting industry veterans to weigh in on its impact and the risks taken by its creators.

During the post‑screening Q&A, director Amir Bar‑Lev praised the film’s willingness to “push the boundaries,” noting that its blend of satirical tone and investigative rigor offers a fresh template for future documentaries. “I’m really happy that your film is doing as well as it’s doing because I think it pushes the boundaries and we all learn from it,” Bar‑Lev told Fielder, underscoring the collaborative spirit that drove the project’s experimental approach. The sentiment was echoed by Oscar‑winning documentarian Chai Vasarhelyi, who highlighted the unprecedented box‑office turnout: “It was kind of like the most …” she said, gesturing to the swelling audience numbers that have turned a niche courtroom story into a cultural phenomenon.

Fielder’s presence on the festival stage marked a departure from his usual behind‑the‑scenes role. Known for his deadpan humor in the television series “Nathan for You,” he has rarely spoken publicly about his filmmaking philosophy. When asked how his comedic background informed the documentary’s tone, he explained that the decision to intersperse irony with factual exposition was intentional, aimed at “making the audience feel the absurdity of the real‑world drama without compromising the seriousness of the investigative work.” This hybrid style, which juxtaposes archival footage with staged reenactments and off‑beat narration, has sparked debate among critics about the line between entertainment and journalism.

Industry analysts see the film’s success as a bellwether for a new wave of documentaries that blur genre conventions. “We’re witnessing a shift where filmmakers are no longer confined to a single aesthetic,” said film scholar Dr. Lila Martinez of Columbia University. “Fielder’s work demonstrates that humor can coexist with hard‑hitting inquiry, expanding the audience base for topics that might otherwise be dismissed as too technical or dry.” The approach also raises questions about ethical responsibility, as some traditionalists worry that comedic framing could dilute the gravity of corporate fraud and its victims’ suffering.

Beyond its artistic implications, “You Can See Everything” has ignited conversations about the broader cultural appetite for true‑crime narratives. The documentary’s box‑office surge mirrors the popularity of podcasts and streaming series that dissect high‑profile scandals, suggesting that audiences crave deeper, more nuanced examinations of power and deception. Executives at major studios have taken note, with several reportedly green‑lighting projects that blend investigative reporting with stylized storytelling—a trend that could reshape the documentary market in the coming years.

Looking ahead, Fielder hinted at potential follow‑ups that could explore other controversial figures using the same “unconventional” toolkit. “If you can take a story that people think they know and make them look at it from a different angle, that’s where the magic happens,” he said. As the documentary continues its theatrical run and prepares for a wider streaming release, its influence on both the craft of nonfiction filmmaking and the public’s engagement with complex corporate narratives appears poised to endure.
